title: Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel
summary:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but […]

The post Melvyn Minnaar: Initmate art encounters in Riebeek-Kasteel appeared first on winemag.
content:
With Swartland acknowledged as the modern classic appellation of the art of wine, it is no surprise that a cute village like Riebeek-Kasteel is a hub for artists of many persuasions. In fact, the visual arts bloom throughout the valley. It may be inspired by the delights of the fine, handcrafted wines at hand, but the geography has its own undulating, bright charm.

Then there are the villagers, the people nearby, living in the panoramic country reality.

Over the past decade an annual mini arts festival has been crafted that exemplify and suits harmoniously the community of Riebeek and surroundings: the way they live, work, make art and wine. The romance is real, if the vocation is hands-on and focussed. The tourism appeal is genuine and, yes, great fun.

The special ‘art weekend’ goes by the title of Solo Studios, a delightful headline for a programme in which local artists perform solo by opening their studios for art inspection by visitors. If the ‘solo’ suggests individuality, the reality is that each contributes to a whole lot of arty pleasure over the weekend – powered, no doubt, by the splendid wines from local wineries.

This year, celebrating the tenth anniversary, Solo Studios X has enhanced the draw. It takes place over the weekend of October 23 – 25 and the programme is jam-packed (a premier weekend pass is R450 plus booking fee per person).

The organisers are boasting with more than 60 artists, five galleries taking part with numerous exhibitions, walkabouts, talks and workshops. Gardens have temporary installed sculptures to admire. And something unique to experience this year is a special garden.

Over the years, the artistic endeavours have held up a tradition of variety, engagement and ingenuity – with a strong local root. At the same time, over the years, artists from elsewhere have found the friendly environment of the weekend inviting to participate and show up.

Sophisticated paintings and sculpture sit easily next to works produced in community spirit. This is art for joy.

Ashley Stone, one of the organisers, summed it up. “It is about creating moments of connection – between people and place, artists and audiences, creativity and conversation. There is indeed something special about experiencing art in the Riebeek Valley.”

As a regular in recent years, I can confirm that special upbeat feeling. (And we always seem to have boxes of Marras and Riebeek Valley wines in the boot for the return route.)       

What I like about the project is the local collaboration and professionalism – no highbrow attitude in operation here. Sharing the spirit is a solid foundation for this successful project.

How playful, for example, to join Antoinette du Plessis for a ‘blue and white’ ceramic plate painting workshop? Or make your own print under supervision of well-known artist Judy Woodborne. She hosts a printmaking workshop on dry point etching.

Just talking to artists in their studios, viewing their process, is both educational and enriching – much like a glass of, say, Marras Chenin Blanc.

Every year a new twist surprises, and this year it’s a ‘Garden of Edible Delights’ on offer by the Valley Potager. Designed and created by Jan Seidel in the style of a European vegetable and fruit kitchen garden in the centre of the valley, visitors are invited along its paths to see, smell and admire.

The star of the upcoming event is unusual and special: a commemorative limited edition box set of ten original prints by local artists who have participated since the first Solo Studios event ten years ago. 10 Years, 10 Artists, 10 Boxes were compiled as both as artwork and archive of the festival’s milestone year, destined to be a collector’s item. It will be available for sale during the festival.

No doubt this year’s Solo Studios in one of my favourite villages, together with some of my favourite wines will once again send weekend visitors home with – if not an artwork or two, that fine portfolio of prints and cases of local wines – cheerful memories of a very cultured community.

  • Melvyn Minnaar has written about art and wine for various local and international publications over the years. The creativity that underpins these subjects is an enduring personal passion. He has served on a few “cultural committees”.

Entries are now open for the third annual NFB Old Vine Report, informed by a blind tasting designed to identify the old-vine wines that perform most convincingly in the glass.

The wines will be tasted by editor Christian Eedes, James Pietersen, CEO of Brice & Burnett, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist.

Why enter?

  • Your wine is judged blind, without producer or brand influencing the result.
  • Every entry receives a Winemag 100-point score.
  • The Top 10 receive individual tasting notes.
  • Buyer’s-guide exposure (wine’s ranked by quality relative to price).
  • The report puts your wine alongside other leading examples from South Africa’s heritage vineyards.
  • Best Overall recognition goes to the highest-performing wine in the tasting.

Entry fee: R1,495 per wine, including VAT.

To qualify, wines must be made from grapes grown on Certified Heritage Vineyards: vineyards aged 35 years or more, registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project.

Entries close 7 October 2026. No late entries will be accepted.

Enter now.


The NFB Old Vine Report is made possible by NFB Private Wealth Management, established in 1985 – because time is the one advantage no investor can buy back.

Winner benefits

The producer of the wine judged Best Overall wins a FERMTECH SOLUTIONS organic fermentation kit worth approximately R10,000 and shipping services worth R10,000 from Aspiring Couriers.

content:
The results of the latest Prescient Fund Service Reports are in, and now you have the opportunity to taste some of the Cape’s most exciting Chardonnays, Cabernet Sauvignons and Bordeaux red blends under one roof.

For one evening only, we bring together a carefully curated line-up of wines that stood out in our latest blind tastings, with the people behind them on hand to talk about how they were made.

Expect wines from producers including Blaauwklippen, Delaire Graff, Diemersdal, Ernie Els, Tokara, Vergelegen and Vrede en Lust.

Among the wines to be poured will be Cavalli Chardonnay 2025, Babylonstoren Cabernet Sauvignon 2024 and Alto M.P.H.S. 2022 – a chance to taste some of the Cape’s most highly rated current releases without having to visit half the province to find them.

This isn’t a formal sit-down tasting. It’s wine without the snobbery: walk around, taste at your own pace, compare bottles, discover new favourites and chat to the people behind them.

And if you find something you love, Getwine will be on hand to help you buy it.

Only 100 tickets are available.

Tuesday 6 October | 17:00–19:00
Welgemeend | Cape Town
R350 per person

Come thirsty. Come curious. Bring someone who likes wine.

Book now.

title: Editorial: The great wine glass con
summary:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous. To be fair, good glassware does […]

The post Editorial: The great wine glass con appeared first on winemag.
content:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous.

To be fair, good glassware does make wine taste better. The problem is that it does not make it that much better.

Consider the South African prices. A pair of Riedel Veloce Cabernet/Merlot glasses available from merchant Reciprocal is R1,345. A two-piece Gabriel-Glas Gold Gift Set from Brice & Burnett is R1,750. A pair of Zalto Balance glasses from Great Domaines will set you back R2,190. At these prices, the wine is no longer necessarily the expensive bit.

The economics of fragility

There is something wonderfully peculiar about the economics. Wine is a consumable: you drink it and buy more. The glass, by contrast, is supposed to be durable. Yet the premium end of the market has engineered these objects to the absolute precipice of structural integrity – making a durable household asset into a slow-burn consumable not because it wears out, but because it is terrifyingly fragile.

This is where the extended cost of ownership enters the picture. First, you buy the glasses. Then you spend the rest of your life worrying about them. You buy the hardware once, but you pay a lifetime subscription fee in pure, unadulterated anxiety. Or, as is unfortunately the case in Chez Eedes, you just keep having to buy new hardware…

The seriousness game

Then, there is the second great trick: ceremony. A wine glass does not merely hold wine. At a certain price point it starts telling others how seriously you take wine. There is a correct bowl, a correct stem, a correct way to hold it, a correct angle at which to examine the colour and, presumably, an incorrect way of drinking something that is ultimately the fermented juice of grapes.

The danger is that the glass becomes part of wine’s unfortunate tendency to turn pleasure into performance. Wine is already burdened with enough ceremony. We have appellations, vintages, viticulture, oenology, typicity and the person at the table who says “there’s a mineral note” before anyone has actually taken a sip. Do we really need a glass that makes wine appreciation feel like a screening process?

The irony is that a good glass is genuinely useful. A generous bowl gives volatile compounds somewhere to go. A narrower rim allows the liquid to hit your tongue just right. Thin glass feels nicer against the lips. Shape affects how wine arrives on the palate. These are not imaginary benefits. But there is a difference between better and transformative.

A R200 glass can be good. A R500 glass can be very good. A R1,000 glass can be lovely. The leap from “lovely” to “this has fundamentally changed my understanding of Pinot Noir” is where I become suspicious.

And what, culturally, are these prices actually connected to? In South Africa, R1,345 is a meaningful amount of money. R2,190 is more than many people would spend on a bottle of wine, let alone the apparatus through which they intend to drink it. The price therefore does not simply represent glassmaking skill. It represents aspiration, design, scarcity, brand mythology and the idea that serious wine requires serious equipment.

Wine has a curious habit of taking a perfectly reasonable proposition – a better glass can improve the experience – and extending it until the proposition becomes you need this particular glass to experience wine properly.

Use good glasses. By all means. If you enjoy the feel of them, the look of them, the ritual of them, spend the money. Pleasure is not required to pass a cost-benefit analysis. But let us stop pretending that a R1,095 glass delivers five times the pleasure of a R219 glass simply because it costs five times as much.

The post Groot Constantia appoints new CEO appeared first on winemag.
content:
Edo Heyns.

Groot Constantia, the commercial wine property held in trust for the nation, has appointed Dr Edo Heyns as CEO, effective 19 October 2026. He will work alongside current CEO Jean Naudé during a handover before Naudé retires on 30 November, having led the estate since 2002. Heyns was CEO of Allée Bleue from March 2024 and previously held senior roles at Advini South Africa. His experience spans wine production, operations, sales, marketing and hospitality.

title: Tim James: A visit to Callie Louw’s Sonkop
summary:
Fans of Callie Louw – there are many, and I think “fan” is the right word – will be pleased to know that all is going well at his new venture. Very well indeed, I’d say after my visit to his farm and nascent winery last week, on a misty spring morning. It’s just more […]

The post Tim James: A visit to Callie Louw’s Sonkop appeared first on winemag.
content:
Fans of Callie Louw – there are many, and I think “fan” is the right word – will be pleased to know that all is going well at his new venture. Very well indeed, I’d say after my visit to his farm and nascent winery last week, on a misty spring morning.

It’s just more than a year since Callie and family arrived here, having left Porseleinberg. There he’d made fifteen vintages of syrah off those vines, and overseen and planted vineyards on this and two other large Swartland properties, all owned by Boekenhoutskloof. It seemed right, as he approached 50, to take the brave and difficult step of working for himself. As he told me at the time: “I’ve always loved farming and owning my own land has been a dream… the fire has grown bigger.”

This new farm – it was called Uitvlucht and has been renamed Sonkop for its highest peak – is in a part of the Swartland that’s remarkably different from Porseleinberg. Rolling hills too, but this is in the Joubertskloof in the low foothills of the Paardeberg, on the other side of that magical mountain from the famous establishments of Sadie, Badenhorst, Lammershoek, David & Nadia et al. With the highest vineyards at about 400 metres, it’s actually more elevated than Porseleinberg. When we drove up to those dizzy heights, Callie assured me that were it not for the mist we’d be able to see right across to Table Mountain.

This is perhaps the prettiest part of the southern Swartland, though lacking the grand vistas of wheatfields and huge open skies with mountains on the horizons. Anyone who knew the Fynbos Estate, home to Johan Simons’s eccentric and occasionally fascinating Dragonridge range of wines, will know this tucked-away area – Sonkop is its neighbouring farm. (A large Rainbow Chickens property is on another side, mostly undeveloped land as far as I could see). 

It’s easy to understand what drew Callie here, even apart from the appealing setting and the attractive buildings, including a good house, amongst large trees. There were already some vineyards planted on the mostly east- but also south-facing slopes, the orientation keeping them a little cooler, less exposed to the afternoon sun. Many vines were virused and needed to be removed (some were grafted to other varieties), but there’s some really good chenin, going back to the 1980s. The farm has a well-sized dam, fed by run-off from the slopes – a significant advantage over the farms of the Aprilskloof and Siebritskloof. Rather too much run-off on rare occasions, in fact – the mighty rains of May this year did fill the dam but also caused some havoc among the bare soils of newly-planted vines.

So. Having lost his viticulturist heart, Callie found a financial partner – always a tricky business, and I gather it took two shots, to find the KwaZulu-Natal wine lover, with some relevant experience in agricutural investment, who is now involved (but keeping his head low for the present it seems). Callie seems very pleased with the arrangements.

Investment in Sonkop is substantial. It’s altogether a much larger proposition than I’d guessed it to be. And larger than Callie had originally thought, in fact. A neighbouring wine-grape farm (devoted to mass production) had come up for sale and Sonkop has shared the land with the recently new owners of the Fynbos estate (things are clearly moving in this sliver of Swartland). These are an Italian-Swiss couple, who are, I gather, more interested in expanding and developing Fynbos’s olive plantations – though they’re not abandoning the vineyards there and, with Callie Louw as a friendly neighbour, can they avoid dabbling in wine too?

Sonkop has, then, a total of some 130 hectares. About 20 hectares of vineyards are now in production – including that old chenin as well as some chardonnay and cabernet sauvignon. Callie has already planted 15 more (shiraz, grenache and more cab), and another 15 will go in next year. White-wine grapes will account for just 12 of the final 50 hectares. Another venture on the farm sees Callie’s wife Marie, a professional photographer, moving to develop a commercial flower garden. Meanwhile, a production cellar is under construction and might just be usable to vinify the grapes that are now mere potential in the vigorous vineyards around it – Callie seems more concerned about getting the paperwork involved in registering it as a wine-production site done in time than the construction logistics.

As to the wines, Callie’s determination is to have just two, expressive of Sonkop and its plantings, and named for it: a red blend – seemingly with a basis in shiraz, and including that surprising cabernet (unorthodox for the modern Swartland) for structural support; and a white blend based on farm’s old chenin. This is a brave ambition; no other significant Swartland producer has managed to achieve this degree of focus – and it’s not the best time in the history of wine to be introducing a new brand, from a fair-sized large farm, with just two wines.

The first Sonkops will be vintage 2026. Callie made them in the cellars of Vondeling, where he is also helping with the wines and vineyards (he doesn’t like the word “consultant”). There they are resting and maturing – sadly I didn’t get a glance or a taste on this visit. Vintage 2027 will, hopefully, be accomplished in the new cellar. The labels for the two Sonkops are being designed now: they will reflect the view of the mountain and vineyards, and the image will, as I understand it, develop in detail and completeness over the next decade as the new vineyards come into maturity.

Callie has been working hard here, and effectively, and there is much more to come – he has, says his friend and former employer Marc Kent, “a work ethic second to none”. When he was showing me the vineyards he’d planted, his pleasure and anticipation was almost palpable as he welcomed the new spring growth of his emerging vines.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

The post Recipe: Cape Malay chicken curry appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with basmati rice and sambals.

Yield

This recipe serves 4 people.

Cape Malay chicken curry recipe ingredients

  • 1 tbsp (15ml) olive oil
  • 1 onion, finely chopped
  • 1 clove of garlic, crushed
  • 1 chilli, deseeded and finely chopped
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) fresh ginger, finely chopped
  • 2 tsp (10ml) coriander
  • 2 tsp (10ml) cumin
  • 1 tsp (5ml) turmeric
  • 1 tbsp (15ml) garam masala
  • 1 x 400g tin tomatoes
  • ½ cup (125ml) chicken stock or water
  • 600g chicken pieces
  • ½ cup (125ml) coconut milk or plain yoghurt
  • 2 tbsp (30ml) chutney
  • salt and freshly ground black pepper
    squeeze of lemon juice
    10g fresh coriander, chopped

Cooking method

  1. Heat oil in a pot and sauté onion, garlic, chilli and ginger for about 2 minutes. Add coriander, cumin, turmeric and garam masala and fry for further few minutes to release their flavours. Add tomatoes and stock and bring to a simmer.
  2. Add chicken and cook, covered, for 20-30 minutes, or until cooked through. Stir in the coconut milk and chutney. Season with salt and pepper and a squeeze of lemon juice.
  3. Serve curry with basmati rice and sambals. Garnish with freshly chopped coriander.

Wine pairing

This dish will work well with a white wine that has some residual sugar, a more full bodied Chenin Blanc an ideal match. Dare we say it, an IPA from your favourite craft brewer will also do the job.

This isn’t a formal sit-down tasting. It’s wine without the snobbery: walk around, taste at your own pace, compare bottles, discover new favourites and chat to the people behind them.

title: Editorial: The great wine glass con
summary:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous. To be fair, good glassware does […]

The post Editorial: The great wine glass con appeared first on winemag.
content:
One of the great con jobs of wine is the expensive wine glass. We have spent decades being told that the glass is not merely a vessel but an instrument, that its shape directs aromas, concentrates flavours, softens tannins and somehow elevates the whole drinking experience to something rapturous.

To be fair, good glassware does make wine taste better. The problem is that it does not make it that much better.

Consider the South African prices. A pair of Riedel Veloce Cabernet/Merlot glasses available from merchant Reciprocal is R1,345. A two-piece Gabriel-Glas Gold Gift Set from Brice & Burnett is R1,750. A pair of Zalto Balance glasses from Great Domaines will set you back R2,190. At these prices, the wine is no longer necessarily the expensive bit.

The economics of fragility

There is something wonderfully peculiar about the economics. Wine is a consumable: you drink it and buy more. The glass, by contrast, is supposed to be durable. Yet the premium end of the market has engineered these objects to the absolute precipice of structural integrity – making a durable household asset into a slow-burn consumable not because it wears out, but because it is terrifyingly fragile.

This is where the extended cost of ownership enters the picture. First, you buy the glasses. Then you spend the rest of your life worrying about them. You buy the hardware once, but you pay a lifetime subscription fee in pure, unadulterated anxiety. Or, as is unfortunately the case in Chez Eedes, you just keep having to buy new hardware…

The seriousness game

Then, there is the second great trick: ceremony. A wine glass does not merely hold wine. At a certain price point it starts telling others how seriously you take wine. There is a correct bowl, a correct stem, a correct way to hold it, a correct angle at which to examine the colour and, presumably, an incorrect way of drinking something that is ultimately the fermented juice of grapes.

The danger is that the glass becomes part of wine’s unfortunate tendency to turn pleasure into performance. Wine is already burdened with enough ceremony. We have appellations, vintages, viticulture, oenology, typicity and the person at the table who says “there’s a mineral note” before anyone has actually taken a sip. Do we really need a glass that makes wine appreciation feel like a screening process?

The irony is that a good glass is genuinely useful. A generous bowl gives volatile compounds somewhere to go. A narrower rim allows the liquid to hit your tongue just right. Thin glass feels nicer against the lips. Shape affects how wine arrives on the palate. These are not imaginary benefits. But there is a difference between better and transformative.

A R200 glass can be good. A R500 glass can be very good. A R1,000 glass can be lovely. The leap from “lovely” to “this has fundamentally changed my understanding of Pinot Noir” is where I become suspicious.

And what, culturally, are these prices actually connected to? In South Africa, R1,345 is a meaningful amount of money. R2,190 is more than many people would spend on a bottle of wine, let alone the apparatus through which they intend to drink it. The price therefore does not simply represent glassmaking skill. It represents aspiration, design, scarcity, brand mythology and the idea that serious wine requires serious equipment.

Wine has a curious habit of taking a perfectly reasonable proposition – a better glass can improve the experience – and extending it until the proposition becomes you need this particular glass to experience wine properly.

Use good glasses. By all means. If you enjoy the feel of them, the look of them, the ritual of them, spend the money. Pleasure is not required to pass a cost-benefit analysis. But let us stop pretending that a R1,095 glass delivers five times the pleasure of a R219 glass simply because it costs five times as much.
